Do not write generic caveats such as "one sample cannot prove...", "a single essay cannot rule out...", "cannot confirm persistence", "limits certainty", or "more data is needed". Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.


Additional fidelity rules for this version:
- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
I want to write about noticing, because it seems like a small skill that keeps getting ambushed. We live among so many signals engineered to claim panic, desire, outrage, or purchase that the ordinary world has to shout to be seen. A kettle boils. A neighbor drags a bin across wet pavement. A street tree leans with what looks like intention toward the last coin of light. These things do not trend, and yet they are the substrate of a life. The trick, if there is one, is to practice returning before attention becomes merely a reflex.

There is a kind of map that shows roads and one that shows waterways, rail lines, elevation, land ownership, or the migratory paths of deer. The most flattering map, for the human ego, is the one that shows everywhere we have already decided to go: from desk to doorway, phone to charger, inbox to apology. The more interesting map is the one whose edges dissolve into uncertainty. Here the path narrows. Here an orchard used to be. Here the sidewalk hums because of underground machinery. A life drawn that way is not a grid but a shoreline: revised daily by tide, weather, and walking.

I think of old travel writing, the sort in which nobody could guarantee the next bridge. The uncertainty was not romantic in itself; it was the condition that made observation sharp. When you cannot rely on the route, you notice the smell of rain before it turns the corner, the posture of a person waiting too long, the slight greenish gleam of copper abandoned for decades. Certainty makes the world into furniture. Ambiguity makes it back into weather.

Technology was supposed to expand attention by removing friction. Sometimes it does. I can listen to a lecture recorded on another continent while washing dishes, which would have seemed like a minor miracle to someone alive in 1500. But remove enough friction and motion becomes frictionless too: the mind slides across surfaces without taking hold. Infinite choice can feel like vastness while producing the sensation of being under a low ceiling. The question is no longer only “what is available?” but “what deserves to land?”

One answer is to choose smaller rooms. A garden bed. A notebook. One unfamiliar bus route. A single bird, if birds can be called singular. Small rooms teach proportion. They reveal that expertise is mostly affection joined to repetition. The person who knows the names of grasses in their neighborhood has not escaped the world; they have entered it more deeply. Knowing the difference between chickweed and spurge is not useful in the way a spreadsheet is useful. It is useful like a handshake: it makes relationship possible.

This does not require rejecting modern life or pretending rural fantasy is honest for everyone. Cities are excellent machines for attention if you stop treating them as corridors. The grocer offers a taxonomy of olives from everywhere. The apartment block contains opera practice, grief, sourdough experiments, tax anxiety, and someone training a bassoon through scales. The bus window frames a cinema of side streets. To notice a city is to accept that you will never finish it. That incompleteness is not failure; it is the deal.

Good writing depends on the same austerity. It does not usually come from adding decoration but from removing blur. The exact noun does more than three adjectives. “A dog barked” is different from “a dog with one ear barked as if betrayed by the moon.” The second risks excess, but the risk is the point: the writer is trying to make hearing possible. Strong prose is a lighthouse made of ordinary language—less a decoration on perception than a way of transmitting it.

There is a moral dimension here that is easy to overstate and impossible to ignore. What you repeatedly notice becomes what you believe exists. If your attention is trained only on contempt, the world will oblige by supplying material. If you never look at labor, neighborhoods become backdrops and workers become invisible. If you never look at rest, every hour becomes extraction. Attention is not merely aesthetic; it is a quiet vote for what counts as real.

Still, noticing should not become another achievement to optimize. The moment mindfulness becomes competitive—“I noticed more beautiful clouds than you did”—it has collapsed into the same hunger it was meant to relieve. Better to aim for porousness: to be affected by fewer things with greater clarity. To hear the kettle before it screams. To see the colleague’s pause as information, not absence. To let a park remain a park for six minutes without photographing it.

What I want, perhaps, is a civilization with better seeing in it. Not a perfect one—those are usually drawn by people who have not lived near anyone—but a slightly more awake one. One in which public spaces are designed for lingering, not only moving through. One in which children are taught observation alongside calculation. One in which boredom is permitted to ripen into curiosity rather than being medicated at the first twitch of discomfort.

The world is not hidden. That is the strange part. It is not locked away in alpine lakes or museum basements. It is under the supermarket fluorescents, in the bus queue, in the failing handwriting of a shop sign, in the way evening arrives earlier every week. The task is not to find extraordinary things but to stop agreeing that everything ordinary is background.

A thousand words about anything, as requested, turns out to be about this: permission to pause before appetite does all the seeing. Go outside if possible. If not, look closely at one thing within reach—a cup, a scar, a crack of light. Let it exceed the label. That is where writing begins, and maybe where a humane life does too.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. A lyrical reflective essay builds a consistent voice from concrete observations and carefully extended metaphors.

## Grounded reading
The voice is measured and inviting, moving from the kettle, wet pavement, and street trees toward broad claims about attention and how to live. Its underlying concern is that distraction turns the ordinary world into background—and that noticing can restore relationship, proportion, and care. The closing invitation to look closely at one nearby thing makes the essay’s argument practical rather than merely abstract.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds everyday sensory details, maps and shorelines, frictionless technology, small repeated acts of attention, and the moral consequences of what people notice or ignore. It presents attention as both an aesthetic practice and a way of recognizing other people, labor, rest, and place as real.

## Evidence line
> Attention is not merely aesthetic; it is a quiet vote for what counts as real.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains its concern with attention across recurring images and turns that concern into a clear ethical invitation.
